Exit polls indicate that part of the shift against the party reflected voter anger at the Trump administration. That could make life harder for likely successors who sit in the current leadership, among them Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Vance has tried to put distance between himself and the defeat, as well as a military adventure in Iran that the BBC describes as a political failure for his party. The academic Karen Beckwith, of Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, was quoted by the BBC saying that Vance has been the figure most damaged by the campaign. Rubio has rejected reports that he is weighing a departure from his job before a 2028 bid.

Republicans who sit outside the administration may find it easier to set out their own positions. Senator Ted Cruz, who was not up for election this year, argued that too many party politicians appear indifferent to the economic concerns of voters. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis took a similarly critical line while citing Republican successes in his state.

A French broadcaster’s summary says Democrats face what could become one of the most crowded and unpredictable presidential primaries in decades, with the party still split over whether to move toward the centre or further left. Jim Messina, a former adviser to Obama, told the BBC that dozens of people are already making moves.
items.cav: Vote counting was still ongoing when these reports were published, so the final picture may change. The French source was available only as a short summary, and the description of the Iran operation as a political failure is the BBC’s characterisation rather than an established judgement.
items.op: Midterm winners and losers do not settle who will win in 2028, and voters deserve candidates who explain their plans in public. The party that answers the anger in these results honestly, rather than with slogans, will earn the trust that counts.

items.t: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie handed 200-year prison term over Shakahola deaths
items.s: According to The Guardian, Paul Mackenzie, leader of a Kenyan doomsday movement, has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the deaths of 190 children and one adult. The term follows a conviction handed down in Mombasa about two weeks earlier.
p: Half of the combined term relates to deaths caused by starvation and half to deaths caused by direct violence, the outlet reported. The sentence concludes a case that has been described as one of the worst cult disasters in recent history.

The verdict was delivered in the coastal city of Mombasa, where the court had found Mackenzie guilty roughly a fortnight before sentencing. Prosecutors argued that, through his church, he pressed followers to deprive themselves and their own offspring of food in the belief that this would spare them at the world’s end. Accomplices reportedly used threats and beatings to enforce those instructions.
Investigators recovered bodies showing severe malnutrition. Some were concealed in crude burial pits and others were dumped in toilet pits. Some victims were reportedly buried while still alive.

The affair came to light in 2023, when a tip led police to arrest Mackenzie. Within weeks, excavations had begun in the Shakahola woodland near the coast in south-eastern Kenya. More than 400 bodies have been retrieved, yet most were so badly decayed that only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie rejected the murder allegations and told the court he had never compelled anyone to fast. The court did not accept that defence. Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache, presiding over a hearing that ran for more than eight hours, said some children had been cut off from food while their parents looked on.

Serious questions remain about how he kept operating. Police searched his premises in 2017, and authorities closed his church in 2019, after which police said he moved to Shakahola. He reportedly barred followers from schooling and from hospital care, calling both satanic. The case has intensified demands for stricter supervision of churches and other faith groups in a country where religion plays a prominent public role.

The judgment addressed 191 deaths, while inquiries into more than 200 further deaths are still open. Mackenzie also faces terrorism and other charges linked to the forest, which he denies. Prosecutors further allege that, while in custody, he directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. He has pleaded not guilty in that case.
items.cav: The conviction and sentence are reported here through a single outlet; the sentencing date and whether the terms run concurrently are not stated. The 52 Kwa Binzaro deaths are prosecutors’ allegations, and the 200-plus other deaths under investigation remain unresolved.
items.op: A sentence of this length is the state’s judgment on the killings, but it is not the whole answer. Kenya’s courts have spoken; the public still deserves a clear account of how a man already on police radar in 2017 kept a congregation under his control for years. Accountability must reach the authorities as well as the accused.

items.t: Kenyan court sentences doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years for 191 murders
items.s: A Kenyan court has jailed Paul Mackenzie, who led a doomsday cult, for 200 years over the deaths of 191 people, all but one of them children. Twenty-eight others were convicted alongside him.
p: Judge Diana Mochache handed down 100 years for homicide and a further 100 years for starvation-related offences, according to the BBC. Terms within each category run at the same time, while the two categories run one after the other, producing a combined sentence of 200 years.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie directed followers to fast until death in the belief that this would bring their children to heaven. The judge placed the main responsibility for the deaths on him, describing the episode as one of the deadliest cases of cult activity anywhere in the world.

Mackenzie, who presented himself as a pastor, was arrested in 2023, after more than 400 bodies were uncovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, close to the coast. The inquiry that followed transfixed the country and attracted attention abroad. He also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he rejects.

The state had asked for the death penalty. Mochache accepted that the case qualified for it to be considered, but she chose not to impose it, reasoning that execution would close off any chance of reform. The BBC notes that Kenya has not executed anyone since 1987.

The judge described the killings as deliberate and planned, and said the accused showed no regret, some even announcing they were prepared to starve themselves. A co-accused reportedly told followers that anyone who refused to fast should be pushed toward heaven by force, the BBC reports. Graves inside the forest were given the name of weddings.

Post-mortem examinations found that starvation accounted for most deaths, while others involved suffocation, strangulation or injuries to the head. For some victims the cause could not be established because the bodies had decomposed, and several people died shortly after being rescued because they were badly undernourished.

The case has also raised questions about oversight. Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights concluded that local administrators and police had repeatedly failed to act on the cult’s activities. Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives, said he went to the police in March 2023 and expected an immediate rescue that never came. A commission of inquiry set up by President William Ruto was later ruled invalid on constitutional grounds.
items.cav: The sources give 191 murders but more than 400 bodies were found; the evidence does not explain how the court arrived at its count or how the two figures relate. Wanje’s account of police inaction is his own and is not independently confirmed in the evidence. The evidence does not say whether the sentence can be appealed or whether the separate charges have a timetable.
items.op: A long sentence does not answer the question of how a cult operated for so long under official eyes. Kenya owes the Shakahola families a full public account of which officials knew what was happening, and why they did nothing. Justice has been done in court, but accountability for the state’s inaction remains unfinished.

items.t: Hoax bomb threats force searches and diversions across European flights
items.s: A wave of bomb threats against commercial flights led to searches, diversions and emergency alerts across Europe this week. Authorities said no explosives were found where checks were reported.
p: Hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights across Europe this week, according to live reporting by The Guardian, which said at least 35 planes had been searched or diverted before Friday. Multiple flights were diverted or forced to make emergency landings, prompting security checks and wider disruption.

A Romanian airline, Tarom, flight from Prague to Bucharest was among the latest believed to be affected. The aircraft sent a squawk code of 7700, the general emergency signal, before landing safely in Bucharest. The Dutch military police confirmed that it had checked a KLM flight to Amsterdam after a bomb threat and that no explosives were on board. The statement did not name the flight. Local Dutch media said it had come from Prague, and the Guardian identified it as KL1350 on that basis.

Hungary’s defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook that fighter jets had been scrambled three times to escort civilian flights in Hungarian airspace after reported threats. The alerts included a WizzAir flight from Brussels to Sofia and flights from Prague to Cyprus and Bucharest.

The Prague airport told the Guardian that nine flights had been affected by bomb threats so far that day. A spokesperson said police had taken the necessary security measures and that “Operations at Prague Airport remain unaffected.” Later, the spokesperson told AFP that at least eight flights to and from Prague had been hit, naming incoming routes from Denmark, Spain and the UK and outgoing routes to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and the UK.

Copenhagen police said they had completed checks at the Danish capital’s airport and had been present only as a security measure. They said they did not assess there to be any danger to passengers or others using the airport, and that they were investigating the new threats. A Bulgarian transport ministry spokesperson told AFP that alerts had also been received for two flights to Sofia, and that both had landed safely.

Flight-tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed planes circling near Prague, with at least four holding near the airport. An AJet service from Istanbul diverted to Vienna after several circles over Prague, but the Guardian said there was no suggestion that it was affected by the threats. The Guardian also reported that at least 17 flights had been disrupted, although details from airports and national authorities had become harder to collect. Eurocontrol’s daily counter put the number of flights in Europe that day at 26,709.
items.cav: The sources do not agree on exact numbers: the Prague airport gave nine and then eight affected flights, and the reported total of disrupted flights is “at least” 17 without a full list. The identification of the KLM flight comes from local media, not from the Dutch police. The AJet diversion is not linked to the threats by any source.
items.op: Hoaxes that empty skies and tie up fighter jets carry real costs, and the public deserves to know how they are being handled. Airports and police should publish consistent, timely counts and clear confirmations of what was found. Reassurance without transparency only leaves passengers guessing.

items.t: Iran Widens Diplomacy to Moscow and Gulf as Washington Weighs Renewed Strikes
items.s: Iran is pressing diplomatic channels with Russia and Gulf states while the United States signals it could resume large-scale military action. Tehran has set seven conditions before it will discuss its nuclear programme or reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
p: Tehran's outreach comes as Donald Trump has hinted that Washington could return to full-scale strikes on the Islamic republic. Citing a US official, the news website Axios reported that US Central Command was readying for major operations and was only awaiting instructions from Washington. On Thursday, Trump said the US might need to wipe out what remains of Iran's capabilities, and suggested the world would find out soon whether he acts.

Friction escalated after Iranian forces brought down two American reconnaissance drones near Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after the US had hit targets earlier in the week. Iranian officials have signalled a response should larger American strikes follow.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had passed Washington a fresh nuclear and peace proposal through Qatari intermediaries, but would only weigh it once the US accepts its seven demands. Those demands reportedly include sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to the American naval blockade around Iranian ports near the Strait. Reuters said Washington is reviewing the offer. The US position, by contrast, is that an agreement on Iran's nuclear capacity must form part of any ceasefire before broader talks can resume.

Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's top security official, travelled to Moscow and met Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin carrying a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, though Iranian state media gave no details of its substance. Rezaei called the encounter a highly significant exchange, according to the Iranian embassy. He also said the sides had discussed plans for gas pipelines linking Russia and Iran, which he framed as a remedy for Iran's gas shortages and a route for Russian energy exports to neighbouring countries.

The Financial Times has reported that Russia earlier agreed to provide Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles, despite its own demand for weaponry in the war in Ukraine. The paper based this on a Russian defence manufacturer's production schedule for 2024 and 2025, where the order was logged under a code associated with Iran. Tehran has previously supplied Shahed drones, and Russia has reportedly assisted Iran with supersonic cruise missiles and Verba portable anti-air missiles. Nicole Grajewski of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told the paper the arrangement suggested Moscow was less troubled by Western objections than before.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke on Thursday with counterparts from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Turkiye, Qatar and Oman about de-escalation and regional stability. Oman's foreign ministry said safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz was a central topic. Separately, Russia's Foreign Ministry urged its citizens not to travel to Iran, pointing to lingering risks of renewed escalation. Senior Iranian officials have warned that any state assisting a US attack on Iran would become a legitimate target.
items.cav: The Financial Times figures on the helicopter-mounted launchers come from documents the paper said it examined, and the evidence does not show an official Russian or Iranian response. Iran's claims about its gas refineries and the contents of Rezaei's message from Khamenei remain unverified, and the Kremlin's readout is not described in the sources.
items.op: Diplomacy is welcome, but seven preconditions and open threats of renewed bombing leave civilians and shipping in the Gulf exposed. Any ceasefire should be built on public terms that all sides can be held to. Secret arms deals and closed-door messages make that harder, and the public has a right to know them.

items.t: Russian-linked group denies role in Europe-wide bomb hoax threats to flights
items.s: A group named in hoax bomb threats to Italian airports has denied any involvement, as flights across Europe received warnings this week. No explosives have been found so far.
p: An Aer Lingus flight bound for Rome was redirected to a French military base after receiving a bomb warning. It was one of many alerts reported across the continent this week, including a Ryanair service from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air rotation from Prague to Rome that ended up in Venice.

The “Male State”, an extremist group with misogynistic views, was named in the threats sent to Italian airports. A Telegram account linked to the group and to its founder, Vladislav Pozdnyakov, told the BBC Russian Service that it had no connection to the emails, saying the group had not existed for many years. The same channel claimed that the group had placed explosives on two inbound aircraft, but no independent source has confirmed this.
Russia banned the group in 2021, and Pozdnyakov is thought to be living abroad. In some places the organisation now calls itself “Male Legion”.

The first hoax message, which the BBC has seen, was sent on Thursday morning to several staff members and departments at Aeroporti di Roma, the firm that runs Rome's airports, as well as to accounts at Fiumicino. The sending address seems to be tied to state health services in Bogota, Colombia. The text, written in fluent Italian, said the group had planted explosives on two incoming planes as an assault on what it called Italy's feminist establishment.

Authorities diverted one of those planes to France, and Italian air force jets escorted the other into Rome. Searches found no explosives on either aircraft or on any other flight that reported a threat. A source at the Rome airport operator said such warnings were highly unusual and could not recall anything comparable in recent years.

On Friday, several prominent Irish media organisations also received bomb threats, leading to evacuations. The Irish government said the incidents appeared to be a coordinated effort to cause disruption. It is not clear whether airports or airlines in other countries received the same or similar threats, and at least one Friday warning appears to have been made by phone rather than email.

La Stampa, an Italian newspaper, has asked whether the group is acting as an armed arm of the Russian state, and it appears convinced of the group's responsibility. Bellingcat, which examined the group in 2022, described it as a loud and hostile online supporter of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Italy's defence minister, Guido Crosetto, said a deliberate effort appears to be underway to deepen chaos. He tied the hoax calls to other recent disruptions, including cyber attacks that pushed up supermarket refrigerator temperatures and problems with France's blood supply. Investigators across Europe are still working out who sent the threats and whether they were coordinated or copied by others.
items.cav: The attribution to the group is disputed: it denies involvement, and the claim of responsibility comes from a channel whose authenticity is not independently confirmed. The Colombian link is only described as an apparent connection, and Crosetto's wider linking of incidents is his own assessment.
items.op: Blaming a group before investigators have established who sent the threats risks confusing the public and rewarding whoever sends them. Authorities should publish what they can verify, and newspapers and ministers should separate evidence from suspicion. Trust in air safety depends on clear, checkable facts.

items.t: Bomb threats hit Irish broadcaster RTE as flight disruption spreads across Europe
items.s: Irish public broadcaster RTE evacuated its buildings after a bomb threat on Friday, adding media to the targets of a wave of threats that has disrupted flights across Europe. Dublin hosts a high-level EU meeting two days later.
p: Media organisations in Ireland were drawn into a campaign that had already grounded aircraft across the continent for several days. On Friday, RTE said its premises had been cleared after a threat was received, and other news outlets were also reviewing their security.

An RTE reporter said the group that claimed responsibility for Friday’s threats was the same one that had targeted airlines earlier in the week. Irish Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris told Cork 96FM radio that it remained unclear whether a lone individual or a coordinated network was behind the campaign.

Taoiseach Micheál Martin called the situation “worrying”. He said the Gardaí (Irish police) and the Defence Forces were investigating who was responsible. Martin also asked any organisation that gets a similar warning to treat it seriously and inform the police, so investigators can piece together a fuller picture.

According to RTE’s account of his remarks, Martin said the episode showed how little it takes to disrupt daily life and unsettle people through unconventional tactics. When asked whether the threats were linked to the EU meetings planned for Dublin, he stressed the need to keep those gatherings on schedule, pointing to the number of prime ministers attending and the heavy security planning this demands.

More than two dozen flights were affected by threats this week, and further incidents were reported on Friday. Police in Denmark and the Czech Republic also responded to threats that later turned out to be false. A Tarom service travelling from Prague to Bucharest was warned, yet reached its planned destination before officials concluded the threat was baseless.

Police in Copenhagen said officers had attended the airport for a second consecutive day in connection with threats aimed at air traffic. They added that passengers faced no danger and that flights had not been disrupted.

The report stresses that bomb threats are not rare, but a run of them in such a short span is out of the ordinary. It sets the episode against rising geopolitical tension with Russia and a string of hybrid attacks that have unsettled Europe. The sources do not say who is responsible or whether any connection to those tensions has been established.
items.cav: The summary describes newsrooms evacuated across Ireland, but the article reports the evacuation only at RTE, with other organisations taking unspecified security measures. The claim that the same group sent threats to airlines and media comes from an RTE reporter and has not been confirmed by officials. Links to Russia are presented as context, not as established fact.
items.op: Threats designed to frighten should not be allowed to hollow out public life. The answer is transparency: officials should explain the investigation as it proceeds, so newsrooms, airlines and citizens can judge the risk rather than guess. Reporting every threat to police, as the Taoiseach urged, is the right instinct.

items.t: Global stocks tumble as tech fears follow Democrats’ midterm win
items.s: Asian markets fell sharply after a heavy sell-off on Wall Street, as investors worried that a Democratic midterm victory could slow the tech investment boom. The Guardian’s live business coverage tracked the losses.
p: Markets across the Asia-Pacific region opened deep in the red after Wall Street suffered steep losses, according to the Guardian’s rolling business coverage. Investors fear that the Democrats’ strong performance in this week’s midterm elections could curb spending on the tech sector’s growth engine.
Japan’s Nikkei lost almost 6%, its steepest one-day fall since April 7 2025, when tariff worries rattled investors. South Korea’s KOSPI slid 6.7%, while Taiwan’s TAIEX shed 4.5%, the report said.

The Guardian reported that more than $3.2tn was erased from the US stock market the previous day. The Nasdaq tech index fell 5.5%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 declined 4.36%.

Makers of memory chips, which had benefited most from the tech spending wave, bore the brunt of the selling. SanDisk dropped 22%, and both Micron and AMD gave up 17% of their value, according to the same account.

Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets, described the session as “a bit of a disaster”. He told Reuters that clients were facing margin calls and complaints, and suggested the shift could signal a wider policy pullback affecting data centres, approvals and equity fundraising.

Analysts blamed policy uncertainty. Democrats have been more critical of data centres, a stance that could slow the build-out of new computing capacity, particularly given public unease about the sector. Kyle Rodda of Capital.com called the selling a “brutal sell-off”.

The Guardian noted that nerves were already present before the vote. Overall earnings have disappointed, with the Magnificent Seven companies falling short of growth forecasts and hinting that spending is cooling. The Nasdaq Composite remains up 4.6% since January, though it is more than 10% below its peak.
Traders are also waiting for the latest US jobs report, which may shed light on the strength of the labour market.
items.cav: All figures and quotes come from a single live-blog summary by The Guardian, and the report links the sell-off to the midterms through analysts’ interpretation rather than direct evidence. The summary does not explain which Democratic policies would be enacted, and the $3.2tn figure is not independently confirmed here.
items.op: Markets are right to question who bears the cost of a tech boom built on lofty valuations. Policy uncertainty should be settled through open rules and public debate, not left to investor panic. Clear, transparent rules for data centres would serve savers far better than sudden swings in sentiment.

items.t: Pope Leo XIV sets off on South America tour, starting in Uruguay
items.s: Pope Leo XIV left Rome on Friday for a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, which DW describes as the longest and farthest trip of his papacy so far. The Vatican says he is in good health, while DW reports that he is recovering from recent cancer surgery.
p: The pope’s departure from Rome took place shortly after 7 am on Friday, according to the Vatican. Leo is due to touch down in Montevideo, the Uruguayan capital, in the late afternoon local time. The Chicago-born pontiff is starting a journey that will also bring him to Argentina and to Peru, a country where he spent years as a missionary and later as a bishop.

Leo’s schedule in Uruguay runs for three days. He will hold talks with President Yamandú Orsi and speak to government officials and diplomats. He is also set to lead Vespers at the Montevideo Metropolitan Cathedral and to visit a neighborhood marked by gang violence. Trips to Paysandú and Florida are planned later in the visit.

From Uruguay the pope moves on to Argentina, with stops in Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján. Euronews names these cities but does not mention political meetings. DW reports that Leo is expected to meet President Javier Milei, whose spending cuts have drawn criticism from the Church for hurting social programmes. DW adds that he also plans to meet business figures, unions and social groups.

In Peru, Euronews lists Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa as stops. DW says the pope will also say Mass in the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba and will go to the Amazon city of Pucallpa to meet indigenous communities. DW also points out that Peru’s Catholic population has dropped from 76% in 2013-2014 to roughly 67%.

Leo’s health is a point of uncertainty. DW says the 71-year-old is recovering from lung cancer surgery performed only three weeks ago. Euronews quotes Maria Montserrat Alvar, the Vatican’s new communications chief, who described the pope’s stamina as excellent and said his doctors feel “very confident”.

DW describes Uruguay as the most secular country in Latin America. It was the first nation to legalise recreational marijuana and has since approved abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying, all over Church objections. Even so, tickets for his prayer vigil at Montevideo’s Centenario Stadium sold out within two days.

DW also notes that Latin America holds about 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, though fewer people there now identify as Catholic. In Argentina, DW cites Pew Research Center figures showing that the share of Catholics fell from roughly 71% at the start of Francis’s papacy to 58% by 2024.
items.cav: Euronews and DW both describe the Peru stops, and DW adds one Mass site, so the two lists do not conflict. Euronews does not mention a meeting with Milei, which appears only in DW, and the cancer surgery is reported by DW alone. The Vatican’s reassurance about the pope’s health comes through a Euronews quotation.
items.op: A papal tour is a religious event, but the public has a fair interest in the health of a 71-year-old leader on a long journey. Official reassurances are welcome, yet they cannot replace clear, direct information. The Vatican should be open about the pope’s condition so that the faithful and observers can judge for themselves.

items.t: Court pauses work on Trump’s Washington arch for two weeks
items.s: A federal judge has put a 14-day hold on building the 250-foot arch Donald Trump wants in Washington, DC. The hold came shortly after a federal planning panel signed off on the design.
p: Judge Tanya Chutkan issued the order on Friday, according to Al Jazeera. The administration had said building could start as early as Thursday, so the pause arrives just before work was expected to begin.
The National Capital Planning Commission backed the project by 8-4 after a nine-hour session on Thursday. Dozens of people who oppose the arch spoke against it during that session.

The decision comes amid several lawsuits against the project. A group of Vietnam War veterans filed one in February. Their filing argues that the arch, planned near Arlington National Cemetery, could obstruct the sightline between the graves and the Lincoln Memorial, a view they describe as deliberately designed to represent national unity.
Trump first floated the arch last year as a way to commemorate the country’s 250th anniversary. He has pointed to Paris’s Arc de Triomphe, completed in 1836, as a model.

The arch is one of several Washington projects Trump has put forward. On Friday he also signed a proclamation turning the Oval Office and Cabinet Room into a national monument. Al Jazeera noted that judges have previously blocked many of his plans, and that Democrats’ midterm victories this week could bring those plans under closer review.
items.cav: The sources describe the pause as temporary and do not say what happens when it ends or how the court will rule on the merits. The veterans’ sightline concerns are claims made in their filing and have not been tested in court. NPR’s summary is brief and does not give the court details or the planning vote.
items.op: Monuments meant to unite a nation should be approved through open, accountable review that gives objectors a real hearing. An 8-4 vote after dozens of objections does not by itself show the process was sound. Courts should test it, and the government should welcome that scrutiny.

items.t: Iranians Uncertain After Trump Midterm Setback as Repression Continues
items.s: Iranian officials have celebrated the Republican midterm losses as a rejection of Trump’s war, while people interviewed inside Iran say they expect repression at home to continue whatever happens in Washington, according to The Guardian.
p: Within hours of the US midterm results, which dealt a heavy blow to the Republican party, supporters of the regime gathered in Tehran’s Enghelab Square and burned a large banner depicting Donald Trump, JD Vance, envoy Steve Witkoff and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Officials have since made combative statements framing the losses as a verdict against Trump’s war on Iran, according to The Guardian.

Supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father Ali Khamenei was killed in strikes in February, declared that the American system was already breaking down. The report adds that state television aired a staged hanging of Trump in Tajrish Square, with an actor wearing a Trump mask and an orange jail uniform.

Among ordinary Iranians the atmosphere is far more guarded. Many point to a deteriorating economy and do not know what Trump’s setback will mean for their lives. Mehnaz, a Tehran-based journalist, described a mood close to hopelessness, with people trying to work out what comes next.

Some of the people Mehnaz has spoken to think the midterm loss raises the risk of a renewed full-scale war, since Trump no longer needs to face voters. She is more worried about the regime itself, which she says has been executing people every day, and she expects that to continue with or without a war.
The Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights (IHR) reports that at least 696 people have been executed in Iran this year. The article does not explain how that count was assembled.

Alborz, a 36-year-old writer in Tehran, describes shops where people still browse but rarely buy, because prices have climbed so steeply that a single T-shirt now costs what a suit did a year ago. He also says people around him believe a full-scale war is less likely now, though he adds that no one can be certain.

Noor, 24, from Karaj, spent three weeks in prison after joining protests in January and says she was arrested during the war. She describes the security apparatus as a “well-oiled machine” that keeps working whatever the state of the conflict. Asked about the days ahead, she said no one inside the country can predict what comes next, adding that people have been bracing for the worst all year.

Moein, a medic in central Iran, says he had underestimated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, both the loyalty of its members and its strategic skill. He sees a painful paradox in a state that has survived decades of sanctions yet turns its coercive power on its own citizens. Mehnaz, for her part, calls the pro-government celebrations increasingly outrageous, arguing that the Guards have found a new reason to hope for survival.
items.cav: The accounts from Tehran, Karaj and central Iran are personal interviews and cannot be independently verified from the article alone. The 696 execution figure comes from a single NGO, and the report does not say whether the mock hanging and official statements reflect wider policy. It also does not say whether the midterm result will change US policy toward Iran.
items.op: Official celebrations of a foreign election loss do not answer the question Iranians face at home: what happens to people jailed and executed by their own state. Transparent counts of executions and steady pressure on Tehran would serve those people far better than bonfires and banners. A regime’s confidence should not be measured by the effigies it burns.

items.t: Irish media outlets evacuate Dublin staff after bomb threats
items.s: Several Irish media organisations moved staff out of their Dublin offices on Friday after receiving bomb threats, Euronews reports. The Irish Independent and broadcaster RTÉ were among the outlets that reported threats.
p: RTÉ said an alert was triggered by an email it received on Friday morning. Staff, including presenters, were led out of buildings on its campus in south Dublin, and officers from the gardaí, Ireland’s police force, went to the site.

RTÉ said its first concern was the wellbeing of its workforce and that it expected to restore its usual output once it had consulted police. Gardaí were also seen at Independent House, the Irish Independent’s headquarters, the newspaper said.
Gardaí told Euronews they knew of a menace aimed at media groups in Ireland and across Europe. They said they were working with the affected outlets and that the threats would be probed.

Taoiseach Micheál Martin described the incidents as grave and suggested they were probably linked to a wider effort to disrupt European life, tied to a recent run of bomb hoaxes against airlines on the continent. He added that it remained unclear who was responsible.

The episode comes roughly a week before Dublin hosts a meeting of the European Political Community. Irish MEP Barry Andrews wrote on X that the summit would address continental security in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and he argued that hybrid attacks are designed to sow confusion and mistrust.
items.cav: The reports do not say who sent the threats or whether any device was found. The Taoiseach’s link to a wider campaign is his assessment, not a confirmed finding, and the details of the threats come to readers second-hand through Euronews.
items.op: Threats aimed at newsrooms strike at the public’s access to information, and they demand a clear account from the authorities. Ireland and its partners should say what they know about this campaign as the investigation proceeds, rather than leave citizens to guess at its purpose. Silence and speculation both serve those who sent the threats.

items.t: Judge halts Trump’s triumphal arch construction for 14 days after contested planning approval
items.s: A federal judge has temporarily blocked building work on a planned triumphal arch in Washington that Donald Trump champions. The order arrived hours after a federal planning panel signed off on the monument.
p: Judge Tanya Chutkan, a US district judge, issued a 14-day temporary restraining order in the early hours of Friday, according to the Guardian. The order stops construction on the 250-foot (76-meter) arch.

The ruling came after a day of government actions. On Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission gave final approval to the structure by an 8-4 vote, at the end of a hearing lasting nearly nine and a half hours. Dozens of witnesses spoke against the plan during that session.

According to the report, the administration had said building could begin once three steps were complete: the planning approval, a final decision from the interior department authorising construction, and a notice published by the National Park Service.

Chutkan agreed to the request of the most recent plaintiffs in lawsuits against the arch. She also combined cases brought by the District of Columbia and Virginia with a case filed by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian.
The report says it is unclear how much the arch would cost or where the money would come from, though some estimates have reached $100m.

The commission’s vote split along federal and local lines. Members backing the project were tied to the administration or to the president, while opponents spoke for the city of Washington. The remote hearing repeatedly malfunctioned early on, and many witnesses argued that the arch would erode the dignity of nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

Mark Paoletta, the commission’s Trump-appointed chair, praised the monument and said Trump was right to want grand monuments. Paoletta is also general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget. Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a General Services Administration lawyer, called the arch “not about politics” but about remembrance and honouring veterans.

Phil Mendelson, a DC council member who also sits on the panel, argued that Congress had not approved the project or appropriated funds for it. He also said the submitted plans omitted the military use that Trump and other officials had cited. Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal, describing it as “a tribute to Donald Trump” rather than to veterans.
items.cav: This account rests on a single outlet, and the restraining order is temporary, so the legal outcome is open. The administration’s stated aims, and claims about congressional approval and military use, come second-hand or from critics. Huffman’s description of the arch is his own opinion.
items.op: A monument of this scale should not advance on the timetable of the official who wants it built, least of all when critics say Congress has neither approved nor funded it. Courts and the public deserve clear answers on approval, cost and purpose before any concrete is poured. Speed is no substitute for accountability.

items.t: Newsom commutes all 548 California death sentences in final months as governor
items.s: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on the state’s death row to life without the possibility of parole, according to his letter and several news outlets. The move means none of them can be executed under future administrations.
p: Newsom announced the decision on Thursday in a letter, saying he was using his constitutional clemency power. The Democrat, who is term limited and is leaving office after eight years, is widely discussed as a possible presidential candidate in 2028.

The Guardian reported that the decision affects 529 men and 19 women. Newsom’s office said 220 of those sentenced have waited 15 years or more for habeas counsel, the lawyers they are entitled to in order to challenge their cases, and 139 have waited 20 years or more. Without the moratorium he imposed in 2019, the office said, 45 people had exhausted their appeals and could have been executed immediately.

In his letter, Newsom wrote that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values. The BBC quoted him saying the state “cannot morally kill them”, and that he believed the state’s death penalty system “is a failure”. He also said he alone bears responsibility for the decision.

California has not carried out an execution since 2006, and the BBC noted that only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978. The Guardian reported that Newsom dismantled the death row chamber at San Quentin prison and moved condemned people to facilities with more freedom of movement.

The announcement came weeks after the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, which the Guardian said had sparked outrage and renewed calls for a nationwide pause on capital punishment. The BBC described it as a botched execution in late September.

Newsom said the California Supreme Court must review and approve clemency for people convicted of multiple felonies. DW, citing the Los Angeles Times, reported that Newsom could commute about 40 percent of the sentences directly, while the court would have to approve 382 others, roughly 70 percent, according to his office.

The American Civil Liberties Union praised the move, as did Bryan Stevenson and Martin Luther King III. Jess Nichol, sister of Polly Klaas, who was killed in 1993, said in a statement that execution had no bearing on her recovery. Governors of both parties have taken similar steps before, including an Illinois Republican who commuted 167 death sentences in 2003.

The federal picture differs. President Donald Trump has described capital punishment as an essential tool, and he reinstated the federal death penalty by executive order in 2025. The BBC reported that no federal executions have been carried out since then.
items.cav: The sources give different figures for how many commutations need court approval: DW and the Los Angeles Times cite 382, while DW’s own 40 percent claim does not add up with that number. The BBC reports that all 548 sentences were converted, while others note the court review requirement, so the final legal status of each case is not clear from these reports.
items.op: Clemency at the end of a term can be legitimate, but it should not depend on one official’s timing or unclear legal process. Californians deserve a complete public account of which commutations are final and which await judicial approval. A justice system that changes with the calendar of a governor’s office is fragile, and the state should set this policy in law.

items.t: Europe's hoax airline bomb threats remain unexplained as Russia suspicions grow
items.s: A wave of bomb threats against European airlines and airports has so far produced no hard evidence of who sent them, according to the BBC. Suspicion has nonetheless fallen on Russia because of other hostile incidents across the continent.
p: The threats arrived in quick succession, each aimed at a different airline or airport. In nearly all cases they were treated as credible enough to divert the aircraft concerned. In Italy, fighter jets were scrambled to escort one flight. London’s Heathrow was a notable exception. Every threat later proved false, though the BBC notes that this does not mean future warnings will be hoaxes.

The simultaneous and co-ordinated pattern has led some people to point to Russia. The BBC describes a run of recent incidents: cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, the remote hacking of supermarket freezers and a blood bank, and a suspicious incident on Poland’s border with Russia. In August, a drone attack on Leipzig Halle airport in Germany was publicly blamed on Moscow by the German interior minister.

Some commentators argue, on circumstantial grounds, that the airline threats fit what is often called hybrid or grey-zone warfare. Such actions damage infrastructure or society while staying anonymous and deniable, and they tend to fall short of the threshold that would trigger Nato’s Article 5 collective defence clause.

The BBC reports that Moscow is angry at Nato’s support for Ukraine. Russian bloggers have also argued that if Ukrainian drones are making Russian airports unsafe, and Western sanctions keep Russian airlines out of European airspace, Western countries should feel similar pain.

Still, as of Thursday evening, no hard evidence had emerged linking the hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups they control. One email, sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome and signed “Fighters of the Male State”, may refer to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion, an ultra-right group banned by a Moscow court in 2021. The BBC notes that the group kept tens of thousands of followers on Telegram. It also warns that the name could be used by another group, and that even a genuine email is unlikely to give police the leads they need.

The BBC argues that national police, airport authorities and transport ministries should not start from their assumptions about the likeliest culprits. Instead, they should follow concrete leads, if they can find them.
items.cav: This is a single-outlet analysis, and the BBC itself says there is no hard evidence linking the hoaxes to Russia, Iran or proxies. The link between the Rome email and the Muzhskoi Legion is described as likely, not confirmed, and the email could come from another group.
items.op: Without proof, blaming a hostile state is a shortcut that can damage public trust and distort the investigation. Authorities owe passengers a transparent account of who is responsible and what evidence supports it. Speculation should not replace detective work.

items.t: Met police urge more victims to come forward as Russell Brand faces two further rape allegations
items.s: The lead detective in the case against Russell Brand has urged other possible victims to come forward, after it emerged the comedian is under investigation for two further rape allegations. Police say files have gone to the Crown Prosecution Service.
p: Brand, 51, was convicted at Southwark crown court of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women over five years, during the peak of his career, according to the Guardian. Jurors cleared him of two other rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault after a four-week trial.

Det Supt Andy Furphy, who leads the Metropolitan police’s work on the case, called Brand a predator whose conduct grew more serious as his profile rose. Speaking after the verdict, he said he believed further victims might exist and that the inquiry was still active.

The force confirmed that Brand had been questioned under caution over two more rape allegations, each made by a different woman. A spokesperson said the files had been passed to prosecutors and that detectives were in regular contact with them. The inquiry, Operation Actinolite, drew on more than 100 witnesses, over 1,400 documents and more than 340 statements.

Pre-trial legal papers, as reported by the Guardian, pointed to outstanding charges linked to a woman who spoke about Brand in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary. She alleged he groomed her while she was a 16-year-old schoolgirl. Furphy would not discuss open lines of inquiry, but urged anyone affected by Brand to contact officers, promising specialist support.

Brand also faces civil proceedings in London and the United States. One woman, who began a claim at the High Court in London, says he assaulted her at his Los Angeles home in 2008, removing her clothing and trying to force oral sex. Brand denies the allegations, which his lawyers have called “fundamentally dishonest”. The claim, lodged last year and paused until the criminal trial ended, reportedly seeks damages of up to £100,000.

Furphy described the verdict as a possible turning point that could encourage others to report sexual crimes, and linked the period to a wider lad culture. He also said Brand had come close to the limits of acceptable conduct during the trial through his podcasts and media appearances, without crossing them.
None of the new allegations or civil claims has been tested in court. The police have not said when, or whether, charging decisions will follow.
items.cav: The reports of further allegations and outstanding charges come from police statements and pre-trial documents as relayed by the Guardian, and the report of other women making allegations is second-hand. The civil claim details come from court papers, and Brand’s denial is given through his lawyers.
items.op: Public confidence depends on keeping convictions, open investigations and unproven civil claims clearly separate. The police appeal for witnesses is right, but every complainant and the accused deserve a fair process. Fame should never shield anyone from scrutiny, and it should never replace evidence in court.

items.t: Cancer diagnoses in England reach record high, but NHS still misses key waiting-time targets
items.s: More than 373,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024, the highest annual figure on record. Experts say the health service is still missing its targets for diagnosis and treatment speed.
p: England recorded its highest cancer diagnosis total yet in 2024, with the latest registration statistics putting the figure above 373,000 people. Averaged out, that works out to more than 1,000 new diagnoses each day, as reported by The Guardian.
The daily average rose to 1,021 in 2024, compared with 972 the year before. Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers made up roughly half of all new cases.
There was also some progress on how advanced cancers were when detected. Around 56.7% of first-time cancers were caught at stage 1 or 2 in 2024, up from 55.8% in 2023.

Prof Peter Johnson, the NHS national clinical director for cancer, described the trend as heading in the right direction and credited frontline staff. He said testing is increasingly being brought nearer to patients who need it.

Specialists urged restraint. Monthly NHS data for August showed 78.6% of urgent suspected-cancer referrals were diagnosed or cleared within 28 days, short of the 80% goal. Only 71.9% of patients began treatment within 62 days of an urgent referral or consultant upgrade, far below the 85% target.

Dr Ian Walker of Cancer Research UK argued that too many people are still diagnosed late and that the NHS needs more help to reverse this. He urged the government to follow through on its national cancer plan for England, which committed to better early diagnosis, faster waiting times and wider access to treatment.

Dr Hilary Williams of the Royal College of Physicians pointed to an ageing population and obesity as contributors to the rise, with obesity described as a significant risk factor that is often underestimated. Steven McIntosh of Macmillan Cancer Support warned that the national picture hides ongoing inequalities linked to where people live and who they are. Rachael Franklin of Breast Cancer Now encouraged women to attend screening when invited.
items.cav: The diagnosis totals are an annual count for 2024, while the waiting-time figures cover only August. The report does not say how much of the increase reflects population growth versus better detection, and the commentators quoted are clinicians and charity representatives rather than independent analysts.
items.op: A record number of diagnoses is not, on its own, a success. If the NHS is finding more cancers while missing its own 28-day and 62-day targets, patients are bearing the cost of that gap. The government should publish a dated plan with named accountability for closing it.

items.t: Paraguayan president resigns as Ueno Bank collapse leaves millions without access to their savings
items.s: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned on Thursday as a banking crisis deepened, just as lawmakers moved to impeach him. The collapse of Ueno Bank has cut off access to accounts for nearly three million customers.
p: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned on Thursday amid a banking crisis, according to Euronews, just as the Chamber of Deputies was voting to impeach him. He announced his decision in a video posted to X while lawmakers were debating his impeachment. He said he was stepping down in the interest of the stability of the country and social peace.

The crisis centres on Ueno Bank, which the central bank took control of on Tuesday, citing a severe capital shortfall. The lender had close to three million customers, who suddenly found their accounts out of reach. Its app, cards and transfers stopped working, and branches locked their doors, leaving depositors queuing outside with no way to withdraw their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open accounts at other banks crashed their mobile apps, adding to public panic.

Regulators investigating the bank reported poorly documented lending and expenses that had been wrongly recorded as assets. Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital fell below the legal minimum, which led to the seizure. Euronews said the size of the shortfall was described in the reporting only in general terms.

In a video, Peña apologised to the public and said he had never intended to betray their trust. He expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the crisis, which has plunged a country long valued by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil. He had held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank until last year.

Ueno grew from an obscure finance company into a household name in less than five years. After receiving its banking license in 2023, it offered cash-back deals on groceries, expanded to more than 70 locations and sponsored the national football team. It claimed more than 60% of Paraguay’s adults as customers. Peña also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the bank’s predecessor, to run the central bank, which supervises the lender.

Public money was heavily concentrated at the bank. As of last month, Ueno reported about $800 million (€712 million) in public deposits, roughly a quarter of its total, including funds from the state pension and health fund. ABC Color reported that central bank inspectors had found a pattern of risky lending to insiders in June. Euronews also reported that nearly $39 million (€35 million) went to three companies tied to the owners on a single day in September 2025. Peña dismissed such concerns as a smear campaign as recently as last month.

Anger has spilled onto the streets. Long lines formed at Ueno branches in the capital, Asunción, on Tuesday and Wednesday, and protesters marched to Congress. One protester, Luis Pineda, accused Peña and the Colorado Party of stealing all savings. Ruling party deputy Alejandro Aquilera said more than three million Paraguayans had been harmed. Vice President Pedro Alliana is set to take office, according to the summary of the report.
items.cav: The sources differ on the sequence of events: the article says the resignation came as the impeachment vote was under way, while the summary says Peña was impeached after resigning. Alliana’s succession appears only in the summary, and the size of Ueno’s capital shortfall is not quantified. The inspection findings and the insider-lending figures are second-hand, relying on ABC Color and the reporting of Euronews.
items.op: Paraguayans were promised stability, and the state’s own pensions and health funds were left exposed. Transparency at the central bank and clear accountability for the president’s ties to Ueno are now essential. Warnings were ignored for months, and no official should be allowed to dismiss scrutiny as a smear.

items.t: US tech stocks slide as investors bet on tougher rules after midterm results
items.s: The Nasdaq was on track for its worst day in 18 months on Thursday, as investors priced in possible tighter rules for the technology sector’s datacentre expansion after the US midterm elections.
p: The Nasdaq composite slumped by as much as 5% in volatile trading on Wall Street, according to The Guardian, and tumbled into what the paper described as “correction territory”, more than 10% below its recent record high. The tech-heavy index was heading for its biggest one-day fall since the tariffs Donald Trump announced in April 2025.

The sell-off was led by chip stocks. The memory maker SanDisk fell 19% and the hard drive maker Western Digital dropped 16.5%. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the tech boom, was the biggest faller on the Dow Jones industrial average, down 6.7%, followed by Goldman Sachs at 5.7%.

Analysts pointed to expectations that Democratic governors will restrict the rollout of new datacentres after the party won a series of gubernatorial races this week. Voters in several local ballots across the country had also rejected datacentre projects, the report said. Worries over heavy spending on datacentres spread to other stock markets worldwide.

The Dow was down more than 1,500 points, or 2.8%, in early afternoon trading, at 51,868 points, while the S&P 500 fell 3.7%. The VIX, Wall Street’s so-called fear index, jumped 40% to its highest level since the early weeks of the Iran war. Britain’s FTSE 100 closed 0.4% lower at 10782.66 after an early rally faded.

The fall reversed a strong rally on Wednesday, when US stocks posted their biggest daily gain in months on hopes that the Democrats’ midterm success could restrain the White House. Trump had celebrated record highs on Truth Social, writing that the stock market had just hit another record and that retirement accounts were “through the roof”.

Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, described a “complete capitulation-level event” in tech stocks. He said the market was selling everything and that it needed to find some stability first. Tech analyst Dan Ives warned that Democrats taking control, especially of the Senate, would create significant hurdles for technology legislation over the next two years, and that the pace of datacentre buildout would slow.

Ted Parkhill, founder and CEO of Incline Investment Management, said the market was moving from promise to price in the tech boom. He added that not every stock tied to the boom was priced appropriately at present, and that there would be a lot of turmoil ahead.
items.cav: The figures are intraday readings from early afternoon trading, so the final closing moves may differ. The expected crackdown on datacentres is based on analysts’ expectations and voter results; the sources do not describe any specific new rule or which governors would act. Ives’s warning about the Senate is his own forecast.
items.op: Markets are pricing in a policy shift that has not yet been written into law, and that is the real problem. Investors reacting to expected scrutiny of datacentres deserve clear rules, a transparent process and a timetable, not rumours of a crackdown. Predictable regulation serves both the industry and the voters who have already said no.

items.t: Russell Brand convicted of rape and sexual assault by London jury, to be sentenced Monday
items.s: Comedian and actor Russell Brand has been found guilty by a London jury of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He denies the charges, was remanded in custody, and is due to be sentenced on Monday.
p: A jury at Southwark Crown Court in London returned its verdicts on Thursday after a four-week trial. Brand, 51, was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of two other rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault, according to the BBC and Al Jazeera.

The offences were said to span 1999 to 2009, the years in which Brand rose from stand-up work in small venues to television and Hollywood success. Prosecutors described him as a ruthless and manipulative sexual predator who used his fame to pressure women. Reports differ on the detail: the BBC says six women gave evidence, while Euronews describes four women and offences between 2005 and 2009.

The jury of eight men and four women deliberated for more than eight hours over two days, according to AFP. Brand closed his eyes and showed little emotion as the verdicts were read, the reports say. He has denied all the charges, saying the encounters were consensual or that the allegations were reinvented after a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and reporting in The Sunday Times.

Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand to expect a “significant custodial term”. He refused bail, citing Brand’s “considerable resources” and the risk that he might not return for sentencing. The judge said he regretted the hardship to Brand’s children, whom Brand had wanted to see over the weekend.

The Metropolitan Police said its investigation into further complaints “remains ongoing”. The BBC and The Guardian report that Brand is under investigation for two further rape allegations, and The Guardian says police have sent files to the Crown Prosecution Service. These claims have not been tested in court, and no further charges have been reported.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy praised the women who came forward, saying their bravery made the outcome possible. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, had argued that the alleged victims waited years to go to police and that the media coverage made a fair trial impossible. Outside court, Winter also made a remark to Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin that drew attention, according to The Guardian.
The maximum penalty for rape in the UK is life imprisonment, Euronews reports. Brand’s sentence will be decided by the judge on Monday, and the convictions remain subject to any appeal.
items.cav: Sources disagree on the number of women, the time span and some counts, so the figures here are attributed to specific outlets. The further allegations are reported as under investigation, not as charges, and the Euronews reference to a 16-year-old complainant is second-hand.
items.op: A conviction shows that fame offers no shield from the criminal law, and that principle matters more than the celebrity. Sentencing should now rest only on what the jury found. Any further allegations must go through the same open, evidence-based process before anyone is judged on them.

items.t: Hoax bomb threats disrupt dozens of European flights as officials weigh possible links
items.s: Hoax bomb threats forced planes into emergency landings and diversions across Europe on Thursday, and officials are still examining whether the incidents were coordinated. No device was found on any affected aircraft.
p: Threats on Thursday disrupted at least 25 flights, according to one report, and some aircraft were forced into emergency landings. Routes touched Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia. Airlines involved included Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet and LOT Polish Airlines. Every plane landed safely, and searches turned up nothing suspicious.

A separate count from DW put the number at a minimum of a dozen commercial flights that landed unscheduled or under high alert, citing national authorities. The two tallies do not match, and neither offers a single consistent figure.

In Britain, Heathrow and Birmingham airports received overnight warnings, which specialist police investigators judged to be hoaxes. The Metropolitan Police said four aircraft linked to Heathrow had been targeted, and a police spokesperson said that after an assessment no security issues had been identified.

The day followed a similar wave on Tuesday, when seven planes were searched or diverted, and a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted on Monday. Counting all of these, one account puts the total for the week at no fewer than 33 affected flights.

Investigators said they still had no evidence that a hostile terror group or a state such as Russia or Iran was orchestrating the hoaxes, though inquiries across Europe continue. The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to say whether the incidents were connected, while stressing that threats against civilians were unacceptable.

Emails sent to airports in Rome and Sofia were reportedly signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma and a text seen by Agence France-Presse. The movement is described as a Russian far-right group whose founder did not comment on or claim the threats. A Kremlin spokesperson dismissed blaming Moscow as absurd.

Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, argued that the hoaxes amount to what he called under-threshold warfare, deliberately kept below the level at which blame can be assigned. In France, media reports said the pilot of an Aer Lingus flight diverted to Évreux was being questioned after initially refusing to land at a military base.

The episode came days after cyber-attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems. Aviation experts quoted by one outlet said that while fake threats are common, the volume of apparently credible ones points to coordination.
items.cav: The sources disagree on the scale, with 25 flights in one account and at least a dozen in the other. The “Male State” attribution comes from unnamed sources and a text seen by AFP, not from a claim of responsibility, and any link to the fridge attacks is unproven.
items.op: Whoever is sending these hoaxes is betting that uncertainty will do the work for them, and so far it is. Governments should publish what they know about the threats and the evidence for any attribution. Travellers and airlines deserve clear findings, not fog.
